# Worksheet: when to act, and what "best" means

**~45 minutes**

The [chapter](../../chapters/13-interventions-and-optimization.qmd) separated two
layers: a **scenario**, which simulates a policy you have already chosen, and an
**optimization**, which searches over policies against an explicit objective.
Here you build both, and then discover that the second layer has a question
hidden inside it. The policy is fixed in shape — a 50% reduction in transmission
lasting ten time units — and the only decision is *when to start it*.

**How to use this file.** Run cells one at a time with `Ctrl+Shift+Enter`. Cells
marked `# TODO` have a line or two for you to complete; everything else runs as
given. Each part ends with `✓` / `✗` lines that check your answer; a `✗` is
information, not failure, and the collapsed hint below it will get you moving.
An instructor is circulating; ask early rather than staying stuck.

**Part C is the point of the session.** Parts A and B build the machinery, and C
is where the machinery says something you did not expect. If you are running
short, read Part B's output rather than tuning it and make sure you reach C.
Worked solutions are posted at the end of each day. Run `git pull` to collect
them.

::: {.callout-note}
Parameters travel as the plain vector `[β, c, γ, reduction, N]` rather than as a
named tuple, for the reason the chapter gives: the callback mutates one entry in
place with `integrator.p[4] = ...`, and a `NamedTuple` is immutable. The comment
beside each entry is doing the work a field name usually does, so the order
matters. Entry 4 is the policy.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Greek letters you can copy

`\gamma` followed by `Tab` gives `γ` at a Julia prompt, but that completion
often does not fire inside a Quarto file like this one. Copy what you need
from here, or insert it from the command palette with the Unicode Latex
extension described in [Setting up](../../setup.qmd#optional-extras).

| Symbol | Reads as | At a Julia prompt |
|---|---|---|
| `β` | beta | `\beta` then `Tab` |
| `γ` | gamma | `\gamma` then `Tab` |
| `₀` | subscript zero | `\_0` then `Tab` |
| `₁` | subscript one | `\_1` then `Tab` |

A subscript is its own character too: `R₀` is `R` followed by `₀`.

Plain ASCII names work exactly as well if you prefer them.
:::

---

## Setup

The state vector carries a fourth component $C$, cumulative incidence, which
only ever accumulates. It is the bookkeeping that turns a question about the
whole epidemic into a single number to read off rather than an integral to
compute.

Be precise about what that number is. $C$ starts at zero, so $C(T)$ counts the
infections generated *after* $t=0$ and up to the horizon $T$ — it excludes the
ten people already infectious at the start, and it is not the eventual epidemic
total unless $T$ is late enough that transmission has finished. Everything below
uses $T=45$ unless it says otherwise, and Part A checks what difference that
choice makes.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch11-setup
using CairoMakie
using DiffEqCallbacks
using EpiModelingCourse
using Optimization
using OptimizationOptimJL
using OrdinaryDiffEq

check(name, condition) =
    println(condition ? "✓ $name" : "✗ $name — not right yet, see the hint")

baseline = BASELINE_PARAMETERS
u0 = Float64[990.0, 10.0, 0.0, 0.0]        # S, I, R, C
time_grid = collect(0.0:0.1:45.0)
intervention_duration = 10.0
maximum_reduction = 0.5

function policy_sir!(du, u, p, t)
    β, c, γ, reduction, N = p
    S, I, R, C = u
    incidence = β * c * (1 - reduction) * S * I / N
    du[1] = -incidence
    du[2] = incidence - γ * I
    du[3] = γ * I
    du[4] = incidence
    return nothing
end

println("R₀ = ", baseline.beta * baseline.contact_rate / baseline.gamma)
```

---

## Part A — one policy, written out (~12 min)

A scenario is a policy you have already chosen. The callback is how a
rectangular policy gets into a continuous-time solve: `PresetTimeCallback` stops
the integrator at the times you name and runs `affect!` there. Your job is the
body of `affect!` — the line that turns the policy on at $t_1$ and back off at
$t_1 + d$.

Note that `affect!` is called at *both* scheduled times, so one line has to
handle both cases. `integrator.t` tells it which one it is at.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch11-a1
function run_scenario(
    start_time;
    duration = intervention_duration,
    reduction = maximum_reduction,
    horizon = last(time_grid),
)
    stop_time = start_time + duration
    initial_reduction = start_time <= 0.0 < stop_time ? reduction : 0.0
    parameters = [
        baseline.beta,           # 1: β
        baseline.contact_rate,   # 2: c
        baseline.gamma,          # 3: γ
        initial_reduction,       # 4: the policy — this is the one that moves
        baseline.N,              # 5: N
    ]
    function affect!(integrator)
        # TODO: set entry 4 to `reduction` at the start and back to 0.0 at the stop
        integrator.p[4] = 0.0
        return nothing
    end
    callback = PresetTimeCallback(unique([start_time, stop_time]), affect!)
    problem = ODEProblem(policy_sir!, u0, (0.0, horizon), parameters)
    return solve(
        problem,
        Tsit5();
        callback = callback,
        saveat = 0.0:0.1:horizon,
        abstol = 1e-8,
        reltol = 1e-8,
    )
end

no_intervention = solve(
    ODEProblem(
        policy_sir!,
        u0,
        (0.0, last(time_grid)),
        [baseline.beta, baseline.contact_rate, baseline.gamma, 0.0, baseline.N],
    ),
    Tsit5(); saveat = time_grid, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8,
)
reference_start = 8.0
reference_solution = run_scenario(reference_start)

baseline_array = Array(no_intervention)
reference_array = Array(reference_solution(time_grid))

check("the policy switches on and off again",
      reference_array[4, end] < baseline_array[4, end])
check("S + I + R is conserved",
      maximum(abs.(vec(sum(reference_array[1:3, :]; dims = 1)) .- baseline.N)) < 1e-6)
check("cumulative incidence never decreases",
      all(diff(reference_array[4, :]) .>= -1e-10))
check("a policy starting at t = 0 really is a policy",
      Array(run_scenario(0.0))[4, end] < baseline_array[4, end] - 1.0)
check("a zero-length policy is the same as no policy",
      Array(run_scenario(0.0; duration = 0.0))[4, end] ≈ baseline_array[4, end])

(; incidence_none = round(baseline_array[4, end]; digits = 2),
   incidence_reference = round(reference_array[4, end]; digits = 2),
   difference_at_45 = round(baseline_array[4, end] - reference_array[4, end]; digits = 2))
```

Two of those checks guard the corners of the decision range rather than the
reference policy. Entry 4 is initialized to whatever the policy is *doing* at
$t=0$, not to zero, so that a policy starting at the lower bound $t_1=0$ is
already switched on before the first step; and the test is
`start_time <= 0.0 < stop_time` rather than `start_time <= 0.0` so that a
zero-length window at $t_1=0$ still means no intervention. `unique` keeps that
degenerate case from scheduling the same instant twice.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part A, the callback

```julia
integrator.p[4] = integrator.t < stop_time ? reduction : 0.0
```

At `start_time` the integrator's clock is before `stop_time`, so the reduction
goes on; at `stop_time` it is not, so it comes off. One expression, both events.
:::

One further detail is why the array is built with
`Array(reference_solution(time_grid))` rather than `Array(reference_solution)`. A
callback forces the integrator to stop and save at the switch times, so a
solution carrying callbacks has a few more saved points than `saveat` alone would
give, and its columns no longer line up with `time_grid`. Calling the solution as
a function interpolates it back onto exactly the grid you asked for.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch11-scenario
#| fig-cap: "A ten-unit, 50% reduction starting at t = 8 compared with no intervention. The shaded band is the policy window."
fig = Figure(size = (860, 620))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "infectious people")
lines!(ax1, time_grid, baseline_array[2, :]; color = :firebrick, label = "none")
lines!(ax1, time_grid, reference_array[2, :]; color = :steelblue,
       label = "50% from t = 8")
vspan!(ax1, reference_start, reference_start + intervention_duration;
       color = (:steelblue, 0.15))
axislegend(ax1; position = :rt)
ax2 = Axis(fig[2, 1]; xlabel = "time", ylabel = "cumulative incidence")
lines!(ax2, time_grid, baseline_array[4, :]; color = :firebrick, label = "none")
lines!(ax2, time_grid, reference_array[4, :]; color = :steelblue,
       label = "50% from t = 8")
vspan!(ax2, reference_start, reference_start + intervention_duration;
       color = (:steelblue, 0.15))
fig
```

The figure stops at $t=45$, but the epidemic does not. Since $C(T)$ is whatever
has accumulated by the horizon, it is worth asking how much of the reported
benefit survives a longer one. The `horizon` keyword makes that a one-line
question.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch11-a2
susceptibles_when_policy_lifts =
    reference_array[1, findfirst(≈(reference_start + intervention_duration), time_grid)]

long_baseline = solve(
    ODEProblem(
        policy_sir!,
        u0,
        (0.0, 200.0),
        [baseline.beta, baseline.contact_rate, baseline.gamma, 0.0, baseline.N],
    ),
    Tsit5(); saveat = 0.0:0.1:200.0, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8,
)
long_reference = run_scenario(reference_start; horizon = 200.0)

difference_at_45 = baseline_array[4, end] - reference_array[4, end]
difference_at_200 = Array(long_baseline)[4, end] - Array(long_reference)[4, end]

check("the long-horizon benefit is smaller than the T = 45 benefit",
      difference_at_200 < difference_at_45)

(; susceptibles_when_policy_lifts = round(susceptibles_when_policy_lifts; digits = 1),
   R_eff_when_policy_lifts =
       round(baseline.beta * baseline.contact_rate / baseline.gamma *
             susceptibles_when_policy_lifts / baseline.N; digits = 3),
   difference_at_45 = round(difference_at_45; digits = 2),
   difference_at_200 = round(difference_at_200; digits = 2),
   postponed_beyond_45 = round(difference_at_45 - difference_at_200; digits = 2))
```

### A1. Interpret

- The infectious curve rises a second time after the window closes. Explain what
  causes that, using `susceptibles_when_policy_lifts` and the reported
  `R_eff_when_policy_lifts`. (The herd-immunity threshold here is $S^\* = N/R_0$;
  the epidemic can only grow while $R_{\text{eff}}>1$.)
- The suppressed first peak looks dramatic. Compare it with `difference_at_45`,
  and then compare *that* with `difference_at_200`. Of the infections the policy
  appears to prevent by $t=45$, how many does it actually prevent, and how many
  does it merely postpone? Say which of these three impressions a decision-maker
  should be given.

> *Your answer here.*

## Part B — the objective landscape (~15 min)

Now the scenario function becomes an objective. Nothing about the model changes;
what changes is that we are prepared to run it many times and compare.

The signature `incidence_at_horizon(x, _)` is what `OptimizationFunction`
expects: `x` is the decision variable as a *vector*, and the second slot is where
fixed parameters would go if the objective needed any. Here it is ignored. The
name says what it returns — $C$ at the horizon — rather than "final size", which
would claim more than the number supports.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch11-b1
function incidence_at_horizon(x, _)
    solution = run_scenario(x[1])
    # TODO: return the final value of cumulative incidence, state 4
    return 0.0
end

check("the objective returns one number",
      incidence_at_horizon([8.0], nothing) isa Real)
check("it agrees with the Part A scenario",
      isapprox(incidence_at_horizon([8.0], nothing), reference_array[4, end];
               rtol = 1e-8))

candidate_starts = collect(0.0:0.25:25.0)
horizon_curve = [incidence_at_horizon([s], nothing) for s in candidate_starts]

(; grid_best_start = candidate_starts[argmin(horizon_curve)],
   grid_best_value = round(minimum(horizon_curve); digits = 2))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part B, the objective

```julia
return Array(solution)[4, end]
```

Row 4 is $C$, and `end` is the last saved time. A maximum or a final value does
not need the grid interpolation from Part A, because it does not pair the
solution against `time_grid`.
:::

The grid is a diagnostic, not the method. About a hundred ODE solves — this grid
is 101 of them — is affordable in one dimension and hopeless in five, which is
what the optimizer is for. The four pieces below are the same four the chapter
names: objective, derivative rule, starting point and box, method.

`Fminbox(LBFGS())` is a *local* method, so "it converged" is not the same as "it
found the best point in the box". Check it three ways: that it reported success,
that it landed near the grid's best start, and that it achieved the grid's best
*value*. Position and value are separate questions, and a flat objective can pass
one while failing the other.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch11-b2
incidence_problem = OptimizationProblem(
    OptimizationFunction(incidence_at_horizon, AutoFiniteDiff()),
    [reference_start],
    nothing;
    lb = [0.0],
    ub = [25.0],
)
incidence_solution = solve(incidence_problem, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 30)
incidence_start = incidence_solution.u[1]

check("the solver reported success",
      successful_retcode(incidence_solution))
check("the optimizer stayed inside the box",
      0.0 <= incidence_start <= 25.0)
check("the optimizer agrees with the grid on where",
      abs(incidence_start - candidate_starts[argmin(horizon_curve)]) < 0.5)
check("the optimizer agrees with the grid on how good",
      abs(incidence_solution.objective - minimum(horizon_curve)) < 1.0)
check("it beats the reference policy",
      incidence_solution.objective < reference_array[4, end])

(; incidence_start = round(incidence_start; digits = 3),
   incidence_value = round(incidence_solution.objective; digits = 2))
```

Before interpreting the optimum, locate two different peaks. Prevalence $I(t)$ is
the one you see in the figure. Susceptible depletion runs at the *incidence*
rate $\beta c SI/N$, which is a different curve with a different maximum.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch11-b3
baseline_incidence_rate =
    baseline.beta * baseline.contact_rate .*
    baseline_array[1, :] .* baseline_array[2, :] ./ baseline.N

prevalence_peak_time = time_grid[argmax(baseline_array[2, :])]
incidence_peak_time = time_grid[argmax(baseline_incidence_rate)]

check("incidence peaks before prevalence does",
      incidence_peak_time < prevalence_peak_time)

(; incidence_peak_time,
   prevalence_peak_time,
   optimal_start = round(incidence_start; digits = 2))
```

### B1. Interpret

- Acting at $t_1 = 0$ and acting at $t_1 = 25$ are both poor, for *different*
  reasons. Say what each one wastes.
- "Act at the peak" is the common intuition. The cell above reports two peak
  times; the best start time is near one of them and not the other. Say which,
  and explain why *that* is the peak that matters, given that what a window is
  worth depends on how much susceptible depletion it prevents.

> *Your answer here.*

## Part C — a different objective, a different answer (~18 min)

Cumulative incidence is one summary of harm. A hospital planner is at least as
interested in the *peak*, because that is what compares against a bed count. The
model is unchanged; only the number we extract from it changes.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch11-c1
function peak_prevalence(x, _)
    solution = run_scenario(x[1])
    # TODO: return the largest number of infectious people at any time, state 2
    return 0.0
end

peak_curve = [peak_prevalence([s], nothing) for s in candidate_starts]

peak_problem = OptimizationProblem(
    OptimizationFunction(peak_prevalence, AutoFiniteDiff()),
    [reference_start],
    nothing;
    lb = [0.0],
    ub = [25.0],
)
peak_solution = solve(peak_problem, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 30)
peak_start = peak_solution.u[1]

check("the two objectives disagree about when to act",
      abs(peak_start - incidence_start) > 2.0)
check("each optimum is the better one on its own objective",
      peak_solution.objective < peak_prevalence([incidence_start], nothing) &&
      incidence_solution.objective < incidence_at_horizon([peak_start], nothing))

(; peak_start = round(peak_start; digits = 3),
   peak_value = round(peak_solution.objective; digits = 2),
   incidence_start = round(incidence_start; digits = 3))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C, the second objective

```julia
return maximum(Array(solution)[2, :])
```

Row 2 is $I$, and this time you want the largest value over all saved times
rather than the last one.
:::

Now cross-tabulate: what does each optimum cost on the *other* measure?

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch11-c2
comparison = (
    no_policy = (peak = round(maximum(baseline_array[2, :]); digits = 1),
                 C45 = round(baseline_array[4, end]; digits = 1)),
    min_incidence = (peak = round(peak_prevalence([incidence_start], nothing); digits = 1),
                     C45 = round(incidence_at_horizon([incidence_start], nothing); digits = 1)),
    min_peak = (peak = round(peak_prevalence([peak_start], nothing); digits = 1),
                C45 = round(incidence_at_horizon([peak_start], nothing); digits = 1)),
)
```

### The trap

The peak objective has a flat region, and a gradient method cannot see out of
one. Below, the same optimisation is started from four different guesses. Two of
them fail — and nothing in the result announces the failure.

Your `# TODO` is the diagnostic: pick out the start times at which the policy
leaves the peak unchanged from the no-intervention value.

```{julia}
#| label: ws-ch11-c3
function optimize_peak_from(guess)
    problem = OptimizationProblem(
        OptimizationFunction(peak_prevalence, AutoFiniteDiff()),
        [guess],
        nothing;
        lb = [0.0],
        ub = [25.0],
    )
    solution = solve(problem, Fminbox(LBFGS()); maxiters = 30)
    return (guess = guess, start = round(solution.u[1]; digits = 3),
            value = round(solution.objective; digits = 2),
            converged = successful_retcode(solution))
end

attempts = [optimize_peak_from(g) for g in (8.0, 15.0, 20.0, 24.0)]

# TODO: keep only the start times whose peak equals the no-intervention peak
plateau_starts = candidate_starts
plateau_begins = isempty(plateau_starts) ? 25.0 : minimum(plateau_starts)

check("a good starting guess finds the optimum",
      abs(attempts[1].start - peak_start) < 0.01)
check("a late starting guess does not move at all",
      abs(attempts[3].start - 20.0) < 0.01 && abs(attempts[4].start - 24.0) < 0.01)
check("the stuck runs are sitting on the no-policy peak",
      abs(attempts[3].value - maximum(baseline_array[2, :])) < 0.05)
check("every attempt reports success, including the stuck ones",
      all(a -> a.converged, attempts))
check("the plateau is the late part of the range, not the whole of it",
      15.0 < plateau_begins < 20.0 && maximum(plateau_starts) == 25.0)

(; attempts, plateau_begins)
```

Read that fourth check twice. It passes — and it is the reason the trap is a
trap. The two stuck runs are not reporting an error for you to notice; they
report exactly what the two successful runs report.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint — Part C, the plateau

```julia
plateau_starts = candidate_starts[peak_curve .>= maximum(baseline_array[2, :]) - 1e-6]
```

The dot in `.>=` compares element by element and gives a vector of `true`/`false`
you can index with. The small tolerance is there because these are floating-point
numbers that will not be exactly equal.
:::

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ws-ch11-objectives
#| fig-cap: "Two objectives over the same decision variable, with the C(45) optimum marked as a dashed line on both panels and the flat region of the peak objective shaded."
fig = Figure(size = (860, 640))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; ylabel = "C(45), cumulative incidence at t = 45",
           title = "Same model, same decision variable, two objectives")
lines!(ax1, candidate_starts, horizon_curve; color = :darkorange, linewidth = 2)
scatter!(ax1, [incidence_start], [incidence_solution.objective];
         color = :firebrick, markersize = 14)
vlines!(ax1, [incidence_start]; color = :firebrick, linestyle = :dash)

ax2 = Axis(fig[2, 1]; xlabel = "intervention start time t₁",
           ylabel = "peak infectious people")
vspan!(ax2, plateau_begins, 25.0; color = (:grey, 0.2))
lines!(ax2, candidate_starts, peak_curve; color = :seagreen, linewidth = 2)
scatter!(ax2, [peak_start], [peak_solution.objective];
         color = :firebrick, markersize = 14)
vlines!(ax2, [incidence_start]; color = :firebrick, linestyle = :dash)
text!(ax2, 19.0, 120.0; text = "flat: gradient = 0", fontsize = 13)
linkxaxes!(ax1, ax2)
fig
```

### C1. Interpret

- The two objectives recommend start times more than four units apart. Using the
  `comparison` table, state what each choice costs on the measure it is *not*
  optimising, and then say which policy is the right one.
- Two of the four optimisation attempts returned their own starting guess and
  reported convergence. Explain mechanistically why the objective is flat there —
  in particular, why the plateau begins where it does.
- Both failures look healthy: converged, inside the box, plausible number. What
  would you do to catch this, given that grid search does not scale
  beyond two or three decision variables?

> *Your answer here.*
